rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all ten compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing late peaks. The intermediate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.
Shorten the scouting gradient to target a last peak before 10 minutes. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed will reveal how the two critical early pairs respond to gradient steepness.
Test the upper temperature limit to shift selectivity in the nearly coeluting early cluster while retaining a fast gradient. Comparing directly with injection 2 isolates the temperature effect.

Use a shallower gradient at the successful high temperature to improve the remaining R=1.14 pair. The last peak at 7.03 minutes leaves room to increase separation while likely staying below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a higher starting organic fraction to change its selectivity. Keep the successful temperature and short gradient; the first peak should still have room before the unretained region.

Increase the starting organic fraction by another grid step to extend the improvement of the critical pair from R=1.14 to 1.32. The other pairs retain resolution margin, and the run should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Injection 6 achieved the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method while testing the narrow resolution margins in the early cluster.

Narrow the gradient window to recover resolution in the two marginal pairs while keeping the shorter programmed gradient. This slope lies between injections 6 and 7 and should retain much of the time savings without sacrificing full resolution.

Test whether raising the starting organic fraction can shorten the fully resolved method from injection 8 and improve its marginal pair. Monitor the earlier pairs for compression as the first peak approaches the unretained region.

Test the grid point between the fully resolved injection 8 and the faster, marginally unresolved injection 7. This checks whether the gradient can be shortened in practice without losing the maximum CRF.
Test a one-step temperature decrease at the near-optimal fast method to measure local selectivity changes in both critical pairs. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed method with CRF 1.000.

The high-temperature region is locally bracketed, with injection 8 retaining the maximum score. Scout the opposite temperature limit with a fast, broad gradient to test whether reordered early peaks offer an alternative fully resolved method.

Return to 60 C and test a gradient slope between injections 8 and 10 using a shorter, narrower gradient. This probes the full-resolution boundary more finely while keeping the final organic fraction above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Injection 13 still has a pair below R=1.5 despite its rounded CRF of 1.000. Use a modestly shallower gradient to seek more resolution margin than injection 8 while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test whether a shallower gradient restores the early pair that fell to R=1.35 at phi0=0.20, while preserving the improved separation of its neighboring pair. This explores a potentially more robust maximum-score method, with the last peak expected below 10 minutes.

Reduce the gradient slope by one endpoint step to bring injection 15’s R=1.49 pair above 1.5. Its last peak at 7.06 minutes leaves sufficient time margin to seek genuine full resolution without a time penalty.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test whether a shallower gradient at phi0=0.15 provides greater resolution margin in both critical pairs. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, preserving the maximum score if all pairs remain resolved.

Back off one endpoint step from injection 13 to bring its marginal R=1.49 pair above 1.5. This tests a six-minute programmed gradient with a slope between two confirmed fully resolved methods and sufficient final organic strength for the last peak.

Refine between injections 8 and 14 to seek slightly more resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method, with only a small retention-time increase. Keep injection 8 as the speed benchmark and preserve the already achieved maximum CRF.

Test one step shallower than injection 17 to increase the minimum resolution while keeping the last peak below the 10-minute penalty threshold. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this run seeks a larger separation margin at the same maximum score.

Test whether the higher starting organic fraction and shallower gradient can compensate for the selectivity loss at 55 C, yielding a fully resolved lower-temperature alternative. The last peak is expected below 10 minutes; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Steepen the successful 55 C method by one endpoint step to shorten retention while testing its R=1.52 limiting pair. This seeks the fastest fully resolved method in the lower-temperature branch without repeating a previous injection.

Refine the phi0=0.20 resolution boundary with a slope between injections 15 and 16, targeting full resolution in less time than injection 16. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed method attaining the maximum CRF.

Test an intermediate slope between injections 14 and 17 to obtain more separation margin than the fastest method while remaining comfortably below the time-penalty threshold. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, and the maximum CRF is already secured.

Use the final injection for a conservative maximum-score candidate with a slope bracketed by successful methods and ample time margin. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with all ten peaks eluting by 6.04 minutes.
